info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 8.1: Manual Grammatical Parsing, Lemmatization, and TEI Linguistic Markup.

name.text: 01 Question: Words Beyond Strings: Why Editions Need Linguistic Markup

questiontext.text: Why does digital textual scholarship require linguistic markup rather than relying exclusively on exact character string searches?

generalfeedback.text: String searches only find exact character matches; linguistic markup reveals the grammar and word families beneath the text.

answer.text: String searches cannot connect different inflected word forms to their shared dictionary headword or identify parts of speech.

feedback.text: Correct. Simple character matching leaves grammatical relationships and word families hidden; linguistic markup records grammar and lemmas.

answer.text: String searches require supercomputers and are too slow to run on modern laptops.

feedback.text: Incorrect. String matching is fast and computationally simple, but it is blind to grammar.

answer.text: Digital editions are forbidden by TEI guidelines from storing plain character text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI easily accommodates plain text; linguistic markup is an analytical enrichment.

answer.text: Optical character recognition software cannot read printed books without parts of speech.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OCR extracts characters from images; linguistic analysis happens downstream.

name.text: 02 Question: Tokens, Surface Forms, and Dictionary Lemmas

questiontext.text: What is the difference between an inflected surface form on a manuscript page and a dictionary lemma?

generalfeedback.text: Lemmatization links inflected surface words from the manuscript to their standard dictionary headwords.

answer.text: The surface form is the exact spelling written on the page, while the lemma is the standard uninflected dictionary headword.

feedback.text: Correct. The surface form preserves historical spelling (e.g. promis'd), while the lemma is the canonical dictionary entry (promise).

answer.text: The surface form is an uninflected base word, while the lemma is an inflected plural.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lemma is the uninflected dictionary citation headword.

answer.text: The surface form only applies to nouns, while lemmas only apply to verbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both nouns and verbs possess surface forms and dictionary lemmas.

answer.text: The surface form is generated by a computer, while the lemma was written by the historical scribe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The historical scribe wrote the surface form; modern editors assign the lemma.

name.text: 03 Question: The Grammatical Feature List

questiontext.text: What information is recorded in a word's grammatical feature list (FEATS)?

generalfeedback.text: A grammatical feature list records all traits—including part of speech, tense, person, gender, and number—for an inflected word.

answer.text: The specific grammatical traits of the inflected word, such as part of speech, tense, person, number, and gender.

feedback.text: Correct. A feature list captures the bundle of inflectional traits attached to an inflected word form.

answer.text: The physical dimensions and ink chemical properties of the parchment leaf.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are codicological physical traits, not grammatical features.

answer.text: The market price of the manuscript at auction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Valuation data does not belong in linguistic feature lists.

answer.text: The font size and CSS style rules used to display the website.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS formatting is separate from grammatical morphology.

name.text: 04 Question: Tokenization in Real Historical Documents

questiontext.text: Why should contractions like French l'assemblée or English can't be split into separate tokens before lemmatization?

generalfeedback.text: Tokenization must split contracted words so that each underlying word receives its own lemma and grammatical tag.

answer.text: Because each piece represents a distinct underlying word that requires its own lemma and part-of-speech tag.

feedback.text: Correct. Splitting l' into a determiner (le) and assemblée into a noun allows each to receive an accurate dictionary lemma.

answer.text: Because computer operating systems crash if a word contains an apostrophe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers handle apostrophes without crashing; splitting is done for grammatical accuracy.

answer.text: Because TEI schemas prohibit the use of apostrophes in diplomatic transcriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI handles apostrophes easily; tokenization isolates words.

answer.text: Because punctuation marks must always be deleted from digital historical editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation is preserved and tagged with , not deleted.

name.text: 05 Question: Words with Multiple Meanings: Homographs

questiontext.text: How do human editors resolve the grammatical category of homographs like English will or French est?

generalfeedback.text: Human readers use sentence context to pick the right lemma when two different words share the same spelling.

answer.text: By examining the surrounding sentence context and grammatical role of the word.

feedback.text: Correct. Context reveals whether will functions as a helping verb or a common noun, and whether est means is or East.

answer.text: By choosing whichever meaning appears first in an alphabetical dictionary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alphabetical order has no bearing on what an author meant in a sentence.

answer.text: By converting the word to uppercase letters in the TEI transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Casing does not resolve grammatical ambiguity.

answer.text: By deleting the ambiguous word from the historical transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never delete genuine witness words.

name.text: 06 Question: Verbs: Tense, Person, and Agreement

questiontext.text: What is the canonical dictionary lemma for archaic English verbal forms like doth or French imperfect forms like décrétoit?

generalfeedback.text: Verb endings show tense, person, and number; manual parsing identifies both the inflected form and its base dictionary infinitive.

answer.text: The uninflected base verb or infinitive, such as do for doth and décréter for décrétoit.

feedback.text: Correct. The canonical citation lemma for verbs is the base uninflected form or infinitive.

answer.text: The exact surface spelling preserved as a new separate dictionary entry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inventing separate lemmas for inflected variants fragments the dictionary index.

answer.text: The third-person singular past participle form.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard English and French lexica cite verbs under base forms or infinitives.

answer.text: A Latin root from the fifth century.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmas are cited in standard modern forms of the language being edited.

name.text: 07 Question: Nouns and Adjectives: Gender and Number

questiontext.text: How does adjectival inflection in French (such as décrets nationaux) differ from modern English adjectives?

generalfeedback.text: French adjectives change their endings to agree with nouns, while English words mainly show number and possession.

answer.text: French adjectives must change their endings to agree in gender and number with their head noun, whereas English adjectives do not inflect.

feedback.text: Correct. French nationaux agrees with masculine plural décrets; English national does not change endings.

answer.text: French adjectives never change endings, while English adjectives have twelve distinct cases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French adjectives inflect for gender and number; modern English adjectives do not.

answer.text: French adjectives only modify pronouns, never nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives modify both nouns and pronouns.

answer.text: French adjectives are always placed in the teiHeader rather than running text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives occur throughout the running document text.

name.text: 08 Question: Function Words: Determiners, Prepositions, and Conjunctions

questiontext.text: What primary role do closed-class function words (like between, and, and dans) play in historical documents?

generalfeedback.text: Function words link nouns and verbs together into complete, well-structured sentences.

answer.text: They provide the structural grammatical glue that connects nouns, verbs, and clauses into meaningful sentences.

feedback.text: Correct. Prepositions and conjunctions govern syntactic relationships between phrases.

answer.text: They provide the primary creative metaphors and poetic imagery in the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open-class content words carry creative imagery; closed-class words provide grammatical structure.

answer.text: They are temporary filler words that can be omitted from scholarly digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Function words are essential to sentence syntax and legal meaning.

answer.text: They only appear in spoken conversation, never in legal treaties or government decrees.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Function words are pervasive in formal legal and administrative prose.

name.text: 09 Question: The Universal Dependencies Part-of-Speech Tagset

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of the 17 Universal Part-of-Speech (UPOS) tags in Universal Dependencies?

generalfeedback.text: The 17 Universal Dependencies UPOS tags give researchers a shared vocabulary for tagging parts of speech across languages.

answer.text: To provide a standardized set of grammatical labels that work consistently across different human languages.

feedback.text: Correct. The 17 UPOS tags provide a shared grammatical vocabulary for English, French, and other corpora.

answer.text: To replace standard English spelling with computer binary code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UPOS tags are grammatical labels, not binary text encodings.

answer.text: To assign grades to student transcriptions automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UPOS is a linguistic framework, not an educational grading rubric.

answer.text: To force all historical languages to adopt modern English word order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UPOS tags describe grammar without changing historical word order.

name.text: 10 Question: Standard Grammatical Features (FEATS)

questiontext.text: How does Universal Dependencies store detailed grammatical traits like gender, tense, and number?

generalfeedback.text: The FEATS field records specific grammatical details using simple pairs like Gender=Masc and Number=Plur.

answer.text: As standardized attribute-value pairs separated by vertical bars in the FEATS field.

feedback.text: Correct. FEATS uses standard pairs such as Gender=Masc|Number=Plur.

answer.text: Inside secret encrypted files stored on a blockchain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. FEATS values are plain-text attribute-value pairs.

answer.text: By coloring the words green or red in the web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Visual styling is presentation; FEATS is structured linguistic data.

answer.text: By adding hundreds of footnotes to the printed page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. FEATS annotations are structured computational attributes.

name.text: 11 Question: Authoritative Dictionaries as Citation Baselines

questiontext.text: Which scholarly authority serves as the primary citation baseline for historical English lemmas in our course documents?

generalfeedback.text: Every lemma should be checked against an authoritative dictionary, such as the OED for English or the TLFi for French.

answer.text: The Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

feedback.text: Correct. The OED provides the historical lexicographical authority for English headwords.

answer.text: A modern social media hashtag index.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Social media tags lack scholarly historical authority.

answer.text: A bilingual English-Latin pocket phrasebook.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Specialized scholarly editing requires unabridged historical lexica like the OED.

answer.text: A spellchecker plugin on a smartphone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commercial spellcheckers do not provide historical citation baselines.

name.text: 12 Question: TEI XML Word Elements: <w> and <pc>

questiontext.text: How does TEI P5 recommend encoding an individual word token and an adjacent comma?

generalfeedback.text: Use the TEI element to enclose words and the element to enclose punctuation marks.

answer.text: Wrapping the word in and the comma in .

feedback.text: Correct. marks a word token and explicitly marks punctuation.

answer.text: Wrapping both together in a tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. is used for editorial alternatives, not basic word tokenization.

answer.text: Putting the entire sentence in a single milestone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. is an empty line-beginning milestone, not a word container.

answer.text: Deleting the comma so the word can stand alone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation must be preserved and encoded with .

name.text: 13 Question: Adding Attributes: @lemma and @pos

questiontext.text: Where are dictionary headwords and part-of-speech tags stored on a TEI word token?

generalfeedback.text: Adding @lemma and @pos to tags attaches dictionary headwords and grammar tags without altering the original text.

answer.text: In the @lemma and @pos attributes directly on the element.

feedback.text: Correct. records both properties on the word.

answer.text: Inside the file name of the digital image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linguistic attributes belong on the text elements, not image files.

answer.text: In the CSS stylesheet under body font rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CSS controls display styling, not grammatical lemmas.

answer.text: In an unlinked external spreadsheet on a different computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI records linguistic metadata directly on elements.

name.text: 14 Question: Grammar Tags vs. Spelling Normalization

questiontext.text: How should an editor combine orthographic regularization with linguistic lemmatization in TEI XML?

generalfeedback.text: Normalization updates spelling, while lemmatization identifies the base word; in TEI XML, nests inside .

answer.text: Nest the regularization element inside the linguistic element.

feedback.text: Correct. acknowledg'dacknowledged keeps both layers intact.

answer.text: Replace the tag entirely with and discard the historical spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Discarding the historical spelling destroys diplomatic evidence.

answer.text: Put the lemma inside and the part of speech inside .

feedback.text: Incorrect. and hold surface text spellings, not grammatical metadata.

answer.text: They cannot be combined because TEI schemas forbid using and in the same file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI fully supports nesting inside .

name.text: 15 Question: External Feature Links with @ana

questiontext.text: What advantage does stand-off annotation with @ana offer when encoding detailed linguistic features?

generalfeedback.text: The @ana attribute links words to external feature lists, keeping transcripts clean while supporting deep grammatical notes.

answer.text: It points to centralized feature definitions in the header, keeping the primary text clean and readable.

feedback.text: Correct. @ana links tokens to feature libraries, avoiding repetitive inline attribute bloat.

answer.text: It speeds up computer internet connections by compressing audio files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @ana is an XML markup pointer, not an internet compression protocol.

answer.text: It hides the text from readers who do not have an academic degree.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stand-off markup organizes data; it does not restrict access.

answer.text: It automatically translates the document into Spanish.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @ana references grammatical analyses, not language translation.

name.text: 16 Question: Marking Sentences with <s>

questiontext.text: Why is wrapping clauses in TEI elements important for computational grammar analysis?

generalfeedback.text: Wrapping clauses in elements marks sentence boundaries that guide grammatical analysis.

answer.text: Because syntactic dependency relations operate within sentence boundaries.

feedback.text: Correct. Syntactic relationships like subjects and verb objects are bounded by sentence units.

answer.text: Because web browsers cannot render text unless every sentence has an tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers display text with standard HTML tags; is for syntactic segmentation.

answer.text: Because sentences are required to be exactly ten words long in TEI P5.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sentences have natural varying lengths.

answer.text: Because elements automatically erase spelling errors in old documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. marks grammatical sentence boundaries without altering spelling.

name.text: 17 Question: Parsing Walkthrough 1: The 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty

questiontext.text: In the 1752 Treaty clause All Treaties shall be renewed, what is the lemma and UPOS tag for Treaties?

generalfeedback.text: Breaking old legal clauses into tables makes lemmas, parts of speech, and grammatical features clear and simple.

answer.text: Lemma: treaty, UPOS: NOUN.

feedback.text: Correct. Treaties is a plural common noun with canonical singular lemma treaty.

answer.text: Lemma: treat, UPOS: VERB.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Treaties is a noun denoting formal agreements, not the verb treat.

answer.text: Lemma: all, UPOS: DET.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All is the preceding determiner, not the lemma for Treaties.

answer.text: Lemma: renewed, UPOS: ADJ.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Renewed is the following participle verb.

name.text: 18 Question: Parsing Walkthrough 2: The 1791 French Revolutionary Decree

questiontext.text: In the 1791 French phrase L'Assemblée nationale décrète les lois suivantes, how do the adjectives agree with their nouns?

generalfeedback.text: French manual parsing requires tracking gender and number agreement across phrases and mapping verbs to infinitives.

answer.text: nationale agrees with feminine singular Assemblée, and suivantes agrees with feminine plural lois.

feedback.text: Correct. French adjectives inflect in gender and number to match their governing nouns.

answer.text: Both adjectives remain masculine singular regardless of the nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French adjectives must agree in gender and number.

answer.text: nationale is a verb, while suivantes is a preposition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both words function as qualifying adjectives.

answer.text: The adjectives agree with the king rather than the nouns in the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Grammatical agreement is syntactic, linking modifiers to their head nouns.

name.text: 19 Question: Parsing Walkthrough 3: Maud Lewis's Folk Correspondence

questiontext.text: In Maud Lewis's sentence I received your letter today, how is the word your analyzed in Universal Dependencies?

generalfeedback.text: Personal letters follow standard Universal Dependencies tags, recording informal phrasing and everyday vocabulary clearly.

answer.text: Lemma: you, UPOS: PRON, Feature: Poss=Yes.

feedback.text: Correct. Your is a second-person possessive pronoun derived from lemma you.

answer.text: Lemma: letter, UPOS: NOUN.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Letter is the head noun being modified.

answer.text: Lemma: your, UPOS: VERB.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your is a possessive pronoun, not a verb.

answer.text: Lemma: Maud, UPOS: PROPN.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud is the letter writer, not the lemma of the pronoun your.

name.text: 20 Question: Handling Old Spellings During Lemmatization

questiontext.text: When lemmatizing an 18th-century word with an archaic spelling (such as French faisoit or English publick), what should the lemma be?

generalfeedback.text: Always assign a modern standard dictionary headword as the lemma, no matter how unusual the spelling is on the page.

answer.text: The modern standard headword (faire or public).

feedback.text: Correct. Lemmas are always modern citation headwords, connecting old spellings to standard dictionaries.

answer.text: An invented historical lemma that preserves the archaic letters exactly (faisoir or publick).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inventing archaic lemmas breaks dictionary lookups across corpora.

answer.text: The word left blank because old words cannot have lemmas.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical words map to standard lemmas.

answer.text: A Latin translation of the word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmas are cited in the standard form of the document's language.

name.text: 21 Question: Multi-Word Phrases and Titles

questiontext.text: How can an editor group multi-word legal formulas like in witness whereof in TEI XML?

generalfeedback.text: Group multi-word legal formulas with while keeping individual elements for each token.

answer.text: Wrap the group in a element while keeping individual tags for each word.

feedback.text: Correct. groups idioms and multi-word units without destroying word-level tokenization.

answer.text: Delete two of the words and keep only one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting words corrupts the historical text.

answer.text: Merge all three words into a single long string with no spaces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merging words destroys tokenization.

answer.text: Replace the phrase with an emoji symbol.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editions maintain rigorous textual integrity.

name.text: 22 Question: Splitting Contractions for Tagging

questiontext.text: In French clitic contractions like d'accord or English don't, how should tokens be divided for linguistic markup?

generalfeedback.text: Splitting contracted words across separate tags lets each word receive its own lemma and part of speech.

answer.text: Split the string so each underlying grammatical word has its own tag with appropriate lemma and POS.

feedback.text: Correct. Distributing letters across tags preserves text while giving each word an accurate tag.

answer.text: Always delete the apostrophe and join the remaining letters into one word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting characters alters the historical evidence.

answer.text: Treat the apostrophe as a finite verb with lemma apostrophe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation marks are not verbs.

answer.text: Ignore contractions and refuse to parse sentences containing them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Contractions are standard features of natural language.

name.text: 23 Question: Heads and Modifiers: The Heart of Syntax

questiontext.text: In dependency grammar, what relationship exists between the words in the phrase national decree?

generalfeedback.text: Sentences are organized into trees where dependent words connect directly to governing head words.

answer.text: decree is the governing head, and national is the dependent modifier.

feedback.text: Correct. The noun decree anchors the phrase, while the adjective national modifies it.

answer.text: national is the head governing the direct object decree.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives modify nouns, not govern them as objects.

answer.text: Neither word is connected because adjectives cannot relate to nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives depend directly on their head nouns.

answer.text: Both words are sentence roots with no dependencies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Only the central clause verb serves as the sentence root.

name.text: 24 Question: A First Look at Dependency Relations

questiontext.text: Which Universal Dependencies relation tag labels the main finite verb of an independent clause?

generalfeedback.text: Standard relation tags like nsubj, obj, and amod label how words connect to their governing heads.

answer.text: root

feedback.text: Correct. The central governing verb of an independent clause is tagged as root.

answer.text: amod

feedback.text: Incorrect. amod is used for adjectival modifiers.

answer.text: punct

feedback.text: Incorrect. punct is used for punctuation marks.

answer.text: det

feedback.text: Incorrect. det is used for determiners like the and a.

name.text: 25 Question: The CoNLL-U Plain-Text Format

questiontext.text: How many standardized columns are used on each token line in a CoNLL-U format file?

generalfeedback.text: CoNLL-U is the global 10-column text format used to store tokens, lemmas, tags, and syntax trees.

answer.text: Exactly ten columns.

feedback.text: Correct. CoNLL-U files use 10 tab-separated columns for token ID, form, lemma, UPOS, FEATS, and syntax.

answer.text: Two columns: word and definition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CoNLL-U has 10 standard columns.

answer.text: Fifty columns covering all world languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CoNLL-U uses 10 columns across all languages.

answer.text: A variable number that changes randomly on every line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CoNLL-U requires a strict 10-column tabular structure.

name.text: 26 Question: Building Your Manual Ground-Truth Table

questiontext.text: What is the first step in creating your project's 20-word manual ground-truth table?

generalfeedback.text: Your 20-word manual ground-truth table provides the trusted benchmark for testing automated software.

answer.text: Select 20 consecutive words from your primary witness that form complete grammatical clauses.

feedback.text: Correct. Choosing continuous grammatical clauses ensures meaningful syntactic analysis.

answer.text: Ask a chatbot to invent twenty random fictional words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground truth must come from your actual primary manuscript witness.

answer.text: Download a modern news article from the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Course work is anchored in the enrolled historical witnesses.

answer.text: Guess the parts of speech without looking at a dictionary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground-truth creation requires authoritative dictionary verification.

name.text: 27 Question: Writing Rules in LEMMATIZATION_POLICIES.md

questiontext.text: Why must digital edition projects document their annotation rules in a policy ledger like LEMMATIZATION_POLICIES.md?

generalfeedback.text: Document your dictionary sources, capitalization rules, and contraction splits in LEMMATIZATION_POLICIES.md.

answer.text: To record decisions on dictionary authorities, capitalization, and contraction boundaries so annotations remain consistent.

feedback.text: Correct. An explicit policy ledger prevents inconsistent editorial decisions across the text.

answer.text: To satisfy commercial copyright laws when selling the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The policy ledger is a scholarly methodological document, not a commercial contract.

answer.text: Because TEI software will not open XML files without a markdown companion file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML processors parse XML independently; the policy document is for scholars.

answer.text: To prevent other researchers from citing the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly documentation invites transparent review and citation.

name.text: 28 Question: Recording Difficult Readings and Editorial Doubts

questiontext.text: What should an editor do when a historical word in a manuscript permits two equally plausible grammatical readings?

generalfeedback.text: When an old word allows two different readings, record your top choice and note the alternative reading clearly.

answer.text: Record the primary interpretation in the table and document the alternative reading in an explanatory note.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparently logging editorial doubts records genuine philological cruxes.

answer.text: Delete the sentence from the digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting difficult passages destroys historical evidence.

answer.text: Flip a coin and pretend no ambiguity ever existed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly integrity requires acknowledging genuine interpretive cruxes.

answer.text: Replace the word with a modern synonym.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors preserve witness readings rather than rewriting history.

name.text: 29 Question: Getting Ready for Wednesday's Automated NLP Test

questiontext.text: How will today's manual ground-truth table be used in Wednesday's Lesson 8.2?

generalfeedback.text: Today's manual ground truth is the benchmark you will use to evaluate automated tools on Wednesday and Friday.

answer.text: It will serve as the trusted benchmark against which the output of automated NLP taggers will be evaluated.

feedback.text: Correct. Wednesday's computational tagger output will be scored against today's manual ground truth.

answer.text: It will be deleted before Wednesday's class begins.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual ground truth is the reference standard for the entire module.

answer.text: It will be converted into a printed poster for library decoration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The table is an active computational testing asset.

answer.text: It will be submitted directly to a journal for publication without testing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The table forms Step 1 of our three-step comparative cycle.

name.text: 30 Question: The Scholar as the Ground Truth

questiontext.text: Why does computational linguistic analysis in digital humanities ultimately depend on human expertise?

generalfeedback.text: Computers process text quickly, but only human editors possess the historical knowledge to create true ground-truth data.

answer.text: Because algorithms rely on statistical patterns from modern data, while human scholars understand historical language and context.

feedback.text: Correct. Human editors provide the historical and linguistic knowledge that machines cannot invent.

answer.text: Because computers are incapable of processing text files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers process text with tremendous speed, but lack historical understanding.

answer.text: Because human scholars can memorize every word in all world languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholars rely on dictionaries and critical analysis, not superhuman memory.

answer.text: Because university policies forbid computers from connecting to the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital humanities actively leverages modern computational tools guided by human expertise.
